articles.title_zh: Regional relations, modern munitions will poise U.S. to defeat China, Trump pick to lead Navy says
articles.content_orig:
U.S. President Donald Trump delivers remarks on reciprocal tariffs during an event at the White House on April 2, 2025.
China warned Thursday that it reserves the right to take “necessary measures” to retaliate against the Trump Administration’s proposed new tariffs , which have reignited global trade tensions.
“China urges the U.S. to correct its wrong practices and return to the right track of resolving issues through dialogue and consultation,” said He Yadong, spokesperson for the Ministry of Commerce. He added that Beijing “reserves the right to take necessary measures and will resolutely safeguard its legitimate rights and interests.”
The Trump Administration targeted 14 trading partners Wednesday in a slew of new tariffs that are set to come into effect early next year. The levies will be imposed under Section 301 of the Trade Act of 1974 following an investigation led by U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer. The U.S. said the probe had found demonstrations of unfair trade practices and excess manufacturing capacity. Mexico and Norway were not listed in the new proposals, as investigations into their respective trade practices are ongoing. Greer framed the tariffs as a way to “level the playing field for American workers and chart a new, more sustainable course for the world economy.” The Section 301 avenue is a way for the Trump Administration to reinstate many of the tariffs that were deemed illegal and struck down by the Supreme Court in February.
China is facing a 20% tariff, which the Trump Administration said it could double to 40% if Beijing does not adhere to the terms of an existing trade truce with Washington.
Another major U.S. trading partner, Vietnam, is facing tariffs of up to 35%. The country’s Ministry of Industry and Trade said it was in the process of “developing and submitting counter-arguments to the preliminary conclusions and inaccurate opinions and allegations from relevant parties.”
Agathe Demarais, a senior policy fellow at the European Council on Foreign Relations, views the tariff proposals as a pressure point on Southeast Asian economies and their trade relations with the U.S. and China.
She says that many of the region’s economies see a lot of Chinese goods pass through before heading to the U.S. market, with tariffs intended to “make it more difficult for economies like Vietnam to position themselves as collector economies between the U.S. and China,” she tells TIME.
The proposed tariffs are subject to a public notice and comment period, with a hearing set to take place early next year before they go into effect, allowing countries to issue responses and arguments.
Deborah Elms, head of trade policy at the Singapore-based Hinrich Foundation, says the proposed measures are already generating significant “resentment” among trading partners.
On top of that, the proposed rates have prompted uncertainty for major economies as to what Washington could do next. “If the U.S. unilaterally determines that the partner is not living up to expectations, then the number can ramp up higher,” she says. “That doesn't really support trust, and it makes it very hard to plan ahead.”
Amid rising tensions, several trading partners are already following China’s lead in voicing their disapproval over the rates.
Bernd Lange, trade committee chair in the European Parliament, said it was “absurd” the E.U. is facing a 20% tariff. He expressed hope that any enforced tariffs will adhere to the Turnberry agreement signed between Washington and the E.U. last year, which capped U.S. tariffs at 15%.
“Washington’s allegations about E.U. industrial overcapacity are absurd. We’ll now see whether the announced U.S. tariffs comply with Turnberry in practice,” he said. “If Washington breaches its commitments, the E.U. must act swiftly. It has the legal means to do so.”
Elms says the threat to hike rates against economies that already have a trade pact with the U.S. further calls into question “how durable” trade commitments with Washington are.
Overall, the proposed rates are just “one more complication in the relationship with the U.S.” that global partners have to contend with, adds Demarais.
Singapore and Japan also hit back at the prospect of respective 20% tariff rates.
Singapore’s Ministry of Energy, Trade, and Industry said it was “very disappointed” by the assessment and argued that the U.S. Trade Representative’s findings “do not take into account the structure of Singapore’s economy.” Japan’s Chief Cabinet Secretary Minoru Kihara referred to the U.S. tariffs as “regrettable,” insisting that: “Japan does not have any nonmarket policies or practices, or structural excess production capacity in the first place.”
Alongside the sweeping tariffs against 14 trading partners, the Trump Administration published a separate proposal seeking to raise levies on Brazil by specifically targeting its sugar and aircraft exports.
“Imposing an additional, specific tariff on sugar imports from Brazil and an additional 10% tariff on finished aircraft exports from Brazil is intended to help bring Brazil to the table,” said the office of the USTR (U.S. Trade Representative). The announcement came amid stalled trade talks between Washington and Brazil.
The Brazilian government expressed “outrage” over the proposed raising of rates, arguing that it has “been acting in good faith in negotiations” relating to Section 301 with the U.S. for over a year.
“The USTR's unilateral decision constitutes an unacceptable action within the ongoing bilateral negotiation process. Brazil will not yield to this type of threat,” the government vowed in a statement.
It said Brazil would continue to negotiate with the U.S., “without ruling out the possibility of adopting retaliatory measures in response to the illegal and unjust imposition of tariffs on Brazilian products.”
The Trump Administration could face significant pushback from the U.S. Congress next year, as Democrats will take control of both the House and Senate in January following sweeping victories in the midterms.
Senator Ron Wyden of Oregon, who will chair the Senate Finance Committee next year, has vowed to try and overturn Trump’s tariffs.
“This is another blatant attempt by Donald Trump to reconstruct his illegal global tariffs, no matter the cost to American families, workers, and small businesses. Global overcapacity is a serious problem, but Trump’s unilateral price-hiking tariffs are not the solution,” Wyden said in a statement . “As incoming Finance Committee Chairman, I will use every tool at my disposal to end Trump’s tariff chaos and restore Congress’ constitutional authority over trade.”
However, securing a veto-proof majority to rein in Trump’s authority could well prove difficult.
Among the general public, tariffs remain deeply unpopular with Americans. An NBC News exit poll following the midterm elections found that 66% of voters believed Trump’s tariff policies had hurt the national economy.

articles.title_orig: How Pentagon considered using Cold War law to bring Jensen Huang back
articles.title_zh: How Pentagon considered using Cold War law to bring Jensen Huang back
articles.content_orig:
Please refresh the page or navigate to another page on the site to be automatically logged in Please refresh your browser to be logged in
Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.
Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth considered using a Cold War-era law to justify the U.S. government stepping in and forcing Nvidia to reinstate its scandal-hit CEO Jensen Huang , according to a report.
The Washington Post claims Hegseth and his senior deputy Steve Feinberg discussed the prospect of President Donald Trump using the Defense Production Act of 1950 to compel the chipmaker’s board of directors to bring back Huang, a step it did eventually take Monday without the act being invoked.
Hegseth and Feinberg reportedly argued that Huang’s return, following his November 12 resignation after a number of extramarital affairs came to light, was essential to national security given that the U.S. is currently locked in an arms race with China to win dominance of AI .
The Pentagon, however, has pushed back on the report and denies Hegseth made any such a proposal.
The emergency act in question grants the president broad authority to intervene in the private sector in the interest of protecting the economy and has been used in the past to gain control of production lines to supply the military during wartime.
The first Trump administration used it during the Covid-19 pandemic in 2020 to order General Motors to produce ventilators with which to treat coronavirus patients.
“Essentially they could use the DPA to force Nvidia to shift more of its production to military projects,” one administration official cited by the Post said.
It is not clear whether the idea of using the DPA to force Nvidia’s hand ever reached Trump and Vice President JD Vance – who weighed in on Huang’s behalf in the hope of restoring calm to the financial markets – or was ever put to the company, according to the newspaper.
However, a Pentagon official told The Independent : “The conversations described between DOW [Department of War] senior leaders never happened and no such proposal was made by the Secretary, Deputy Secretary, or Under Secretary.”
The president has admitted he and Vance played a pivotal role in persuading the Nvidia board to bring back the 63-year-old, its leader since 1993, who was forced to step down earlier this month when his infidelities were exposed, one of which was with a woman whom U.S. intelligence believed to be a Chinese spy .
Nvidia likewise admitted in a statement it had received input from “senior levels” of government before making its U-turn.
After the decision was announced, Trump cheered Huang’s return , insisting he had done nothing wrong and was a “genius” the country needed to power its AI boom and that there was no concern about his alleged romantic ties to Megaspeed executive Alice Haung (no relation).
“The United States Government has no reason to believe that Jensen’s return to Nvidia poses any risk to National Security,” the president wrote on Truth Social Monday.
“The Attorney General of the United States has confirmed that the U.S. Government does not possess evidence that he has engaged in any unlawful conduct.”
The Post argues that Hegseth’s alleged proposal reveals the “intensity” with which the military currently views the AI race with Beijing, as well as Silicon Valley ’s “growing entanglement” with the Department of Defense.

articles.title_orig: All safe codes in GTA 6 and where to find them
articles.title_zh: All safe codes in GTA 6 and where to find them
articles.content_orig:
In the crime action game Grand Theft Auto VI, numerous caches of cash, rare weapons, and collectibles are hidden throughout the state of Leonidas, access to which is restricted by electronic combination locks or safes. To save time searching for clues, reviewers have compiled a list of fourteen proven combinations covering story locations, warehouses, labs, and gang hideouts. The list includes fixed codes, requiring careful attention to the leading zeros: 7700 for the door to Brian's warehouse, 0420 for the Moonstone Boutique back room, 092319 for the garage of a party house southeast of Key Lento, 44017 for a safe in a trailer near Cottonmouth Lake, and 62412 for an abandoned laundromat in Belleville.
A separate chain of sequential puzzles is located at the research station in Pelican Valley, where rewards are unlocked in stages. First, players must enter the password "CLEAVES" to unlock the lab computer, which provides a hint for the code 0072 for the local safe. The safe's contents allow the door to the dockside barn to be opened with the combination 0212, allowing them to retrieve a special version of the VF5 submachine gun. In addition to fixed passwords, the game features a number of criminal safehouses, where the combinations can change randomly depending on the specific playthrough, so the numbers provided serve as a basic guide when examining notes and photographs.
Six locations fall into the category of conditionally variable locks: 7777 for the Nova Auto junkyard in Hamlet, 0300 for the safe in the Kingpin bowling alley office, 6823 for the safe at Brooks Boatworks, 6969 for the safe at the La Cascara Motel, 6769 for the building on the dock at Sunrise RV Park, and 2121 for the safe in the laboratory at McKittrick Farm. If the code entered from this list doesn't work, players are advised to carefully examine the tables, walls, and documents inside the room to find the correct combination for the current game session without having to guess.

articles.title_orig: Nvidia chip buyers told to rule out Chinese renters to purchase GPUs, sources say
articles.title_zh: Nvidia chip buyers told to rule out Chinese renters to purchase GPUs, sources say
articles.content_orig:
Nvidia chip sellers are seeking new buyers for the semiconductor giant's hardware, three people told CNBC, after the Trump administration tightened rules to curb Chinese companies' remote access to the most advanced artificial-intelligence systems.
Companies have put an unusually high volume of Nvidia graphics processing units, or GPUs, on the market since new measures restricting Chinese companies renting access to advanced Nvidia chips were announced on Nov. 16, the people said.
Jack Duhamel, president of AI infrastructure marketplace GPU Mart, and two people familiar with the matter told CNBC the surge in GPUs for sale was directly attributable to the new rule. Duhamel added that one company looking to sell Nvidia chips told GPU Mart the sale was related to the new rule.
The two people said it appeared chip sellers were seeking to offload them because they were originally for use in data centers in which Chinese companies would rent access. They asked not to be named because they were discussing private information.
The Department of Commerce's Bureau of Industry and Security, or BIS, announced an interim final rule as part of a clampdown on Chinese companies bypassing export controls, which effectively ban the sale of the most advanced Nvidia chips to China, by accessing them remotely in overseas data centers. The rule came into effect on Nov. 19.
Deals to find buyers for thousands of B300 GPUs, one of Nvidia's most advanced offerings, have been floated since the rule was announced, said Duhamel and one of the people.
Nvidia declined to comment. BIS did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
Nvidia has been facing increasing scrutiny from U.S. lawmakers over Chinese companies' access to its advanced chips.
The chip giant warned its customers that the proposed Remote Access Security Act — which has passed the House of Representatives but is yet to pass the Senate — would give the U.S. government broader authority to control access to cloud services, potentially exposing both parties to "legal action," sources previously told CNBC.
In July, the U.S. accused a Chinese AI lab, Moonshot AI , of accessing Nvidia chips via a facility in Thailand. CNBC reported on Nov. 5 that the company had sought access to the chips via data centers in Europe.
U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer told CNBC's "Squawk Box" on Wednesday that the new rule announced last week was intended to close "loopholes."
"For a long time, we have not allowed the sale of Blackwell chips, which are the highest AI chips or similar chips to China directly," he said.
"Some rules were issued by the Commerce Department last week to close off indirect access, either smuggling through places like Southeast Asia or remote access from data centers in third countries."
During Nvidia's third-quarter earnings call on Nov. 17, then-interim CEO Colette Kress said the company was still studying the controls, but expected performance to remain strong because demand for chips far exceeded supply.

articles.title_orig: China and Brazil Lead Pushback Against Trump’s ‘Unacceptable’ Tariff Threats
articles.title_zh: China and Brazil Lead Pushback Against Trump’s ‘Unacceptable’ Tariff Threats
articles.content_orig:
U.S. President Donald Trump delivers remarks on reciprocal tariffs during an event at the White House on April 2, 2025.
China warned Thursday that it reserves the right to take “necessary measures” to retaliate against the Trump Administration’s proposed new tariffs , which have reignited global trade tensions.
“China urges the U.S. to correct its wrong practices and return to the right track of resolving issues through dialogue and consultation,” said He Yadong, spokesperson for the Ministry of Commerce. He added that Beijing “reserves the right to take necessary measures and will resolutely safeguard its legitimate rights and interests.”
The Trump Administration targeted 14 trading partners Wednesday in a slew of new tariffs that are set to come into effect early next year. The levies will be imposed under Section 301 of the Trade Act of 1974 following an investigation led by U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer. The U.S. said the probe had found demonstrations of unfair trade practices and excess manufacturing capacity. Mexico and Norway were not listed in the new proposals, as investigations into their respective trade practices are ongoing. Greer framed the tariffs as a way to “level the playing field for American workers and chart a new, more sustainable course for the world economy.” The Section 301 avenue is a way for the Trump Administration to reinstate many of the tariffs that were deemed illegal and struck down by the Supreme Court in February.
China is facing a 20% tariff, which the Trump Administration said it could double to 40% if Beijing does not adhere to the terms of an existing trade truce with Washington.
Another major U.S. trading partner, Vietnam, is facing tariffs of up to 35%. The country’s Ministry of Industry and Trade said it was in the process of “developing and submitting counter-arguments to the preliminary conclusions and inaccurate opinions and allegations from relevant parties.”
The proposed tariffs are subject to a public notice and comment period, with a hearing set to take place early next year before they go into effect, allowing countries to issue responses and arguments.
Deborah Elms, head of trade policy at the Singapore-based Hinrich Foundation, says the proposed measures are already generating significant “resentment” among trading partners.
On top of that, the proposed rates have prompted uncertainty for major economies as to what Washington could do next. “If the U.S. unilaterally determines that the partner is not living up to expectations, then the number can ramp up higher,” she says. “That doesn't really support trust, and it makes it very hard to plan ahead.”
Amid rising tensions, several trading partners are already following China’s lead in voicing their disapproval over the rates.
Bernd Lange, trade committee chair in the European Parliament, said it was “absurd” the E.U. is facing a 20% tariff. He expressed hope that any enforced tariffs will adhere to the Turnberry agreement signed between Washington and the E.U. last year, which capped U.S. tariffs at 15%.
“Washington’s allegations about E.U. industrial overcapacity are absurd. We’ll now see whether the announced U.S. tariffs comply with Turnberry in practice,” he said. “If Washington breaches its commitments, the E.U. must act swiftly. It has the legal means to do so.”
Elms says the threat to hike rates against economies that already have a trade pact with the U.S. further calls into question “how durable” trade commitments with Washington are.
Singapore and Japan also hit back at the prospect of respective 20% tariff rates.
Singapore’s Ministry of Energy, Trade, and Industry said it was “very disappointed” by the assessment and argued that the U.S. Trade Representative’s findings “do not take into account the structure of Singapore’s economy.” Japan’s Chief Cabinet Secretary Minoru Kihara referred to the U.S. tariffs as “regrettable,” insisting that: “Japan does not have any nonmarket policies or practices, or structural excess production capacity in the first place.”
Alongside the sweeping tariffs against 14 trading partners, the Trump Administration published a separate proposal seeking to raise levies on Brazil by specifically targeting its sugar and aircraft exports.
“Imposing an additional, specific tariff on sugar imports from Brazil and an additional 10% tariff on finished aircraft exports from Brazil is intended to help bring Brazil to the table,” said the office of the USTR (U.S. Trade Representative). The announcement came amid stalled trade talks between Washington and Brazil.
The Brazilian government expressed “outrage” over the proposed raising of rates, arguing that it has “been acting in good faith in negotiations” relating to Section 301 with the U.S. for over a year.
“The USTR's unilateral decision constitutes an unacceptable action within the ongoing bilateral negotiation process. Brazil will not yield to this type of threat,” the government vowed in a statement.
It said Brazil would continue to negotiate with the U.S., “without ruling out the possibility of adopting retaliatory measures in response to the illegal and unjust imposition of tariffs on Brazilian products.”
The Trump Administration could face significant pushback from the U.S. Congress next year, as Democrats will take control of both the House and Senate in January following sweeping victories in the midterms.
Senator Ron Wyden of Oregon, who will chair the Senate Finance Committee next year, has vowed to try and overturn Trump’s tariffs.
“This is another blatant attempt by Donald Trump to reconstruct his illegal global tariffs, no matter the cost to American families, workers, and small businesses. Global overcapacity is a serious problem, but Trump’s unilateral price-hiking tariffs are not the solution,” Wyden said in a statement . “As incoming Finance Committee Chairman, I will use every tool at my disposal to end Trump’s tariff chaos and restore Congress’ constitutional authority over trade.”
However, securing a veto-proof majority to rein in Trump’s authority could well prove difficult.
Among the general public, tariffs remain deeply unpopular with Americans. An NBC News exit poll following the midterm elections found that 66% of voters believed Trump’s tariff policies had hurt the national economy.

articles.title_orig: Union Vote Fails In Landslide At GTA 6 Studio Rockstar Games As 75 Percent Of Devs Vote No
articles.title_zh: Union Vote Fails In Landslide At GTA 6 Studio Rockstar Games As 75 Percent Of Devs Vote No
articles.content_orig:
Grand Theft Auto VI GTA 6 Rockstar Games Union
Rockstar Games will not be forced to formally recognize a union at the Grand Theft Auto 6 studio after its developers based in the UK voted overwhelmingly against the initiative. The weeks-long voting process played out as Rockstar launched the open-world hit to over 30 million sales in its first day .
Voting began on November 12 and concluded today on November 26 . Workers at Rockstar Games voted 75 percent against the recognition agreement with the IWGB Game Workers Union. The initiate would have formalized collective bargaining efforts around things like overtime, bonuses, layoffs, and AI. Developers in favor of unionizing can still work with the IGWB, but there will be no regular meetings with management to hash out new policies.
“We are extraordinarily proud of our team, the culture we’ve built together and the launch of Grand Theft Auto 6,” Rockstar head of publishing Jennifer Kolbe said in a statement shared with Kotaku . “This result reflects our team’s strong support for continuing the direct relationships, collaboration and open dialogue that have helped make Rockstar Games so innovative and strong. As we look ahead, we’re excited to build on all we’ve accomplished together.”
The IWGB Game Workers Union pushing the vote released the following statement:
For anyone at Rockstar who believes in a fairer workplace, a fairer sector and a fairer society – this isn’t a sign to retreat, it’s a sign to double down on what we stand for. Hundreds of our coworkers voted in favor of our union at Rockstar, yet sadly we recognize we have more work to do to build understanding and win the trust of more of our colleagues. We’re ready to put in the effort to make that happen.
Whilst we haven’t emerged with a recognition deal, this ballot has put our union on the radar of every worker, and opened the door for new kinds of conversation to start happening. People entirely unfamiliar with unions were for the first time debating employment conditions, collective bargaining rights, and our contracts. We heard from many more colleagues about what mattered to them, and we hope people will continue to engage so that we can see where these new discussions can lead us.
A recognition agreement would have marked a path towards greater workplace democracy. But it’s one route of many. At Rockstar we have already won, and will continue to win, tangible changes that improve our everyday lives. We’ll keep fighting for a say. For pay transparency, contractual overtime pay, and protections against AI and layoffs.
The power to shape our working lives has always been, and will always be, in our hands.
The vote comes roughly a year after Rockstar fired dozens of developers it accused of gross misconduct and breaking confidentiality rules around the development of GTA 6 . The fired workers accused the studio of union busting, which it has denied, and a legal fight has been ongoing over the last 12 months at a labor tribunal. A final judgement in that case is still pending. As recently as this month, members of both sides of the dispute were testifying on the record for the case.

articles.title_orig: 75% of Rockstar’s workers have voted against unionizing
articles.title_zh: 75% of Rockstar’s workers have voted against unionizing
articles.content_orig:
UK-based Rockstar workers have voted against unionizing.
The IWGB, a union representing some Rockstar workers, has confirmed that workers rejected a deal that would recognize the Rockstar Game Workers Union.
The two-week ballot, which ran from 12 to 26 November, overlapped with the launch of Grand Theft Auto 6 . The results were roughly 25% in favor of recognizing the union, and 75% against, with the vast majority of its around 1,600 employees participating.
Recognition would have established a formal framework for workers to negotiate collectively over pay, overtime, bonuses, leave, pensions, and the impact of AI and redundancies.
The result does not prevent Rockstar workers from organizing with the IWGB or exercising their trade union rights, but means management will not be formally committed to regular meetings with union representatives. The union is also able to continue representing individual members.
The IWGB says that this has not dissuaded them, and they will continue to try and “win the trust” of Rockstar employees.
“For anyone at Rockstar who believes in a fairer workplace, a fairer sector and a fairer society – this isn’t a sign to retreat, it’s a sign to double down on what we stand for,” a statement from the IWGB reads.
“Hundreds of our coworkers voted in favour of our union at Rockstar, yet sadly we recognise we have more work to do to build understanding and win the trust of more of our colleagues. We’re ready to put in the effort to make that happen.
“Whilst we haven’t emerged with a recognition deal, this ballot has put our union on the radar of every worker, and opened the door for new kinds of conversation to start happening,” the statement continues. “We heard from many more colleagues about what mattered to them, and we hope people will continue to engage so that we can see where these new discussions will lead us.
“A recognition agreement would have marked a path towards greater workplace democracy. But it’s one route of many. At Rockstar we have already won, and will continue to win, tangible changes that improve our everyday lives. We’ll keep fighting for a say. For pay transparency, contractual overtime pay, and protections against Al and layoffs.”
In its own statement, Rockstar Games said it was “extraordinarily proud of our team, the culture we’ve built together and the launch of GTA 6.”
“This result reflects our team’s strong support for continuing the direct relationships, collaboration and open dialogue that have helped make Rockstar Games so innovative and strong,” said Jennifer Kolbe, head of publishing. “As we look ahead, we’re excited to build on all we’ve accomplished together.”
This comes amid an employment tribunal into alleged union busting at Rockstar .
In 2025, Rockstar dismissed 34 workers who were active in the workplace’s union efforts. They say they were let go as part of an effort to stop these efforts, whereas Rockstar says they were dismissed for leaking confidential information .

articles.title_orig: Motorola Signature 27 Shipping Slips to December Amid High Demand
articles.title_zh: Motorola Signature 27 Shipping Slips to December Amid High Demand
articles.content_orig:
Getting your Trinity Audio player ready...
Since its unveiling on Nov. 5, the Motorola Signature 27 flagship has generated strong demand in the US smartphone market. It’s rare for a phone outside of Apple, Samsung, or Google to create such a buzz, but Motorola has now been forced to delay shipments for some early orders.
Preorders for the Signature 27 began on Nov. 19, with general availability expected Nov. 26. As reported by 9to5Google , the preorder window is still open on Motorola and Best Buy, but the shipment dates there have slipped to Dec. 8 and Dec. 11, respectively.
“We’re excited by the strong consumer response of the new Motorola Signature 27, with demand exceeding our initial expectations. As a result, some orders may experience updated shipping timelines,” Motorola tells 9to5Google. “Our teams are working to meet demand and get devices to customers as quickly as possible.”
The phone became available in Europe on Nov. 16, and the delay in the US market won’t affect all preorders. Some of the buyers will still receive their units on launch date as promised, Android Authority reports .
The demand for Signature 27 is primarily driven by its mind-boggling spec sheet. The $1,600 Motorola flagship runs on the latest 2nm Snapdragon 8 Elite Extreme Gen 6 chip and comes in two variants: 12GB RAM/256GB storage or 16GB RAM/512GB storage. Its 6.8-inch display offers a 120Hz adaptive refresh rate and reaches a record-breaking 12,000-nit peak brightness.
The 7,000 mAh battery, meanwhile, promises up to 47 hours of video playback and supports reverse charging. The front camera is 50MP, and the rear setup includes a 50MP main shooter, a 200MP periscope telephoto lens with 100x Super Zoom, and a 50MP ultrawide camera. To top things off, the phone ships with Android 17 out of the box and is slated to receive 7 years of OS and security updates.
Specs aside, users are excited about the phone’s support for GrapheneOS , a privacy-focused Android alternative previously limited to Pixel phones. Some of them are also excited about the phone’s potential to increase competition in the US market.
Jibin is a tech news writer based out of Ahmedabad, India. Previously, he served as the editor of iGeeksBlog and is a self-proclaimed tech enthusiast who loves breaking down complex information for a broader audience.

articles.title_orig: U.S. Stock Futures Higher as AI Trade Steadies for Thanksgiving Break
articles.title_zh: U.S. Stock Futures Higher as AI Trade Steadies for Thanksgiving Break
articles.content_orig:
Global stocks rallied on Thursday, staging a tentative recovery from an intense AI-driven sell-off and looked past a fresh set of tariffs unveiled by the White House on Wednesday.
U.S. markets will be closed Thursday for the Thanksgiving holiday and will have a shortened trading session on Friday. During Wednesday's regular session, the Dow gained 0.33%, the tech-heavy Nasdaq Composite fell 0.62% and the S&P 500 shed 0.25%, with the major averages paring losses seen earlier in the trading day.
In Europe on Thursday, equities rose sharply. The pan-European Stoxx 600 was 1.6% higher by 12:20 p.m. in London (7:20 a.m. ET), with all sectors and major bourses in positive territory.
Germany's DAX led gains on a rise of 1.9%, while the Stoxx 600 Technology index jumped 2.5%. The regional tech index has lost around 12% so far this month, amid jitters around a potential AI bubble bursting and the ousting — and return — of Jensen Huang as Nvidia CEO.
German semiconductor firm Infineon was more than 4% higher in afternoon trading, as chip stocks notched a boost. ASMI and ASML each gained just over 3%, while Be Semiconductor added 3.5%.
Asia-Pacific markets also rose on Thursday, with regional tech stocks also rebounded sharply, led by Japanese chip-related companies.
South Korea's Kospi gained 0.29% to close at 4,711.21, while the small-cap Kosdaq index advanced 0.78% to 655.71 after the country's central bank hiked benchmark lending rates to a 2-year high in its final meeting of the year.
Japan's Nikkei 225 rose 0.86% to 57,499.16 while the Topix edged 0.11% higher to 3,750.4. Australia's S&P/ASX 200 gained 0.82% to 8,763.8.
Hong Kong's Hang Seng index was up 1.52% in its last hour of trade, while mainland China's CSI 300 edged higher marginally, closing at 3,900.55.
SoftBank Group surged more than 7%, while chip-testing equipment maker Advantest rose 4.57%. Lasertec and Disco gained , while Tokyo Electron climbed 0.59%
In South Korea, memory chip giants SK Hynix and Samsung Electronics advanced more than 2% and 0.35%, respectively. The gains followed a bruising session Wednesday amid renewed concerns over the sustainability of artificial intelligence spending.
Russ Mould, investment director at AJ Bell, labeled it a "solid day" for regional markets, suggesting investors were hunting for opportunities in the wake of an intense global sell-off.
"The rollercoaster stock market is back on an upwards path as a new round of Trump tariffs aren't as bad as feared and the US takes the day off to celebrate Thanksgiving," he said in a note on Thursday morning. "It was notable that investors cast their net wide for opportunities, fishing for bargains in the rubble following the tech sell-off and looking at other sectors in the quest for diversification."
But Mould warned investors not to be "too complacent."
"Oil prices heading higher is not good for efforts to tame inflation, neither is the prospect of retaliation by countries on the receiving end of new US tariffs," he said.
The Trump administration on Wednesday unveiled a fresh barrage of tariffs on more than a dozen trading partners, including China, the European Union and India.
Daniela Hathorn, senior financial market analyst at Capital.com, said in a Thursday note that the mood in markets was "cautious rather than uniformly negative."
"European markets are attempting to rebound after yesterday's decline, while U.S. cash markets are closed for Thanksgiving, limiting the chance to test whether Wall Street's late recovery can hold," she said. "The main focus now will be trying to determine how many further increases the Fed considers necessary in early 2027 and whether AI shares can withstand that rate path while investors continue to question the returns on heavy spending."
U.S. inflation data on Wednesday reinforced expectations of further monetary tightening by the Federal Reserve. The personal consumption expenditures price index rose 3.8% year on year in October, accelerating from 3.7% in September, while core inflation came in slightly above expectations at 3.3%.
Mark Haefele, chief investment officer at UBS Global Wealth Management, said in a note on Thursday morning that his team believes investors should maintain strategic allocations to equities.
But he advised market participants to "review current allocations and use market moves as an opportunity to rebalance, refocus, and strengthen portfolio resilience."

articles.title_orig: I am staunchly pro-choice – but abortion statistics in the latest sexual attitudes survey shocked even me | Zoe Williams
articles.title_zh: I am staunchly pro-choice – but abortion statistics in the latest sexual attitudes survey shocked even me | Zoe Williams
articles.content_orig:
Young Britons are having half as much sex as they were in 1990, according to a new study, with the average reported frequency falling from four times a month to just twice a month.
The data was produced as part of a long-running study known as the National Survey of Sexual Attitudes and Lifestyles (Natsal), according to a statement Wednesday from the London School of Hygiene & Tropical Medicine (LSHTM), which participates in the research.
“The sex lives of people in Britain have changed markedly since 1990 and they have substantial and varied sexual and reproductive health needs,” LSHTM said.
Researchers randomly selected around 6,700 people from England, Scotland and Wales aged 16-59 to participate in interviews and online surveys between September 2022 and January 2024.
This is the fourth edition of “one of the largest studies of sexual behaviour in the world,” which has previously been undertaken in 1990, 2000 and 2010.
In addition to adults under 45 years old reporting that they are having sex half as much as their peers did in 1990, the survey showed that 77% of 16-59-year-olds reported having sex in the past year, and 89% said they had sex at least once in their lives.
Among 16-24-year-olds, one in three said they had never had sex, up from around one in five in 2010.
Half of young women reported watching pornography in the past 12 months, compared with nearly 90% of male respondents. This was the first time the survey had asked about the use of online pornography.
Attitudes toward children and contraception are also changing. While the use of hormonal contraception declined among young women, the proportion of women who report that they don’t want children has doubled in the past decade.
The survey also reveals important findings for preventing the spread of sexually transmitted infections (STIs), with more than one in four sexually experienced 16-24-year-olds with exclusively opposite-sex partners reporting behaviors that are associated with STI risk.
These include “having four or more partners or condomless sex with two or more partners in the past year or overlapping partners in the past five years,” the statement said.
Men’s sexual health can predict heart issues
“While most adults are having sex, people are having sex less often and more young people have never had sex,” Soazig Clifton, academic director for Natsal at University College London, which also participates in the survey, said in the statement.
“There is also a higher proportion of people reporting same-sex experiences, and online sexual activity is now part of everyday life for many.”
Dr Otilia Mårdh, a scientific officer at the European Centre for Disease Prevention and Control (ECDC), who was not involved in the research, said that “another notable Natsal-4 finding is, that the proportion of men reporting both same-sex and opposite-sex partners (MSWM) more than doubled, from 0.9% (Natsal-3) to 2.3%.”
Feeling like a late bloomer when it comes to sex? There’s hope
“The authors note that this growing population could increasingly bridge sexual networks with different STI risks,” Mårdh said in a comment published by the Science Media Centre on Wednesday.
She added that this is “particularly relevant” as surveillance data from European monitoring programs shows “recent increases in syphilis and gonorrhoea among heterosexual populations, alongside rising congenital syphilis — contrasting with historically lower levels.”
“These trends highlight the need for accessible, stigma-free sexual health services offering prevention and testing tailored to people’s needs,” said Mårdh.
Five papers drawing on the results of the survey were published in the journal The Lancet.

articles.title_orig: Denny's brings back plaque celebrating Nvidia chief Jensen Huang
articles.title_zh: Denny's brings back plaque celebrating Nvidia chief Jensen Huang
articles.content_orig:
Jensen Huang is back at the helm of Nvidia — and Denny's has a booth waiting for him.
The American diner chain welcomed the billionaire's return as Nvidia CEO by revealing that it had reinstated a commemorative plaque marking the birthplace of the artificial intelligence chip giant after learning of its removal on Nov. 13.
"Some things you just don't take off the menu. Jensen Huang is one of them," Denny's said in a post on X .
The plaque marks the booth at a Denny's restaurant in Silicon Valley, California, where Huang and his co-founders discussed the idea for Nvidia, which was founded in 1993.
The restaurant chain said it learned on Nov. 13, a day after Huang's resignation , that the plaque had been removed.
"We put the plaque right back up where it belongs," Denny's said, without specifying who had removed it or why.
Huang's ties to the diner chain, however, stretch back well before Nvidia's founding. He worked at Denny's as a teenager, washing dishes and serving customers before going on to build one of the world's most valuable companies.
The restaurant chain also disclosed that it had contacted Nvidia's communications team on Nov. 10 to express its pride in their shared history.
Huang's return came less than two weeks after his sudden resignation rattled investors and raised questions about corporate governance and succession planning at the chipmaker.
While his return has put those issues in the spotlight, Denny's offered a simpler message to its former employee.
"Jensen, your booth is waiting and the coffee's on. We're always open, 24/7," the restaurant chain said.

articles.title_orig: Trump Tried to Cripple Huawei. Now It Is Central to China’s A.I. Push.
articles.title_zh: Trump Tried to Cripple Huawei. Now It Is Central to China’s A.I. Push.
articles.content_orig:
China’s biggest technology firm and the world’s largest telecommunications equipment maker has been convicted in the U.S. of stealing trade secrets and defrauding banks about its business in Iran.
Huawei was found guilty on 10 of 12 counts by a jury in Brooklyn on Tuesday. The verdict all but brings to a close an almost eight-year-long criminal case against Huawei and three of its subsidiaries. The sprawling legal case spanned a 12-week trial, dozens of witnesses, and hundreds of motions and filings.
It’s a rare case of U.S. prosecutors securing a conviction against a foreign corporation and could have significant consequences for both Huawei and U.S.-China relations.
The Justice Department first announced charges against Huawei in January 2019 as part of the first-term Trump Administration’s “China Initiative,” a controversial program to investigate and prosecute Chinese influence and espionage in the U.S.
The Shenzhen-based tech giant was found guilty of bank and wire fraud, conspiracy to steal trade secrets, and violations of U.S. sanctions. It faces massive potential penalties, including fines, forfeiture, and restitution. Sentencing is set for September 2027, with motions in advance of sentencing expected to start in the third week of January.
“Few crimes are as serious as Huawei’s decades-long pattern of endangering U.S. national security, violating the sanctity of U.S. commerce, and impeding the enforcement of U.S. laws,” U.S. Attorney Joseph Nocella Jr. said .
James Barnacle Jr., assistant director in charge of the FBI’s New York office, added, “Huawei’s success was built on deception and theft, and the FBI will never hesitate to pursue those who profit by breaking the law.”
The jury, however, acquitted Huawei of the most serious charge: racketeering conspiracy under the Racketeer Influenced and Corrupt Organisations Act (RICO).
Huawei’s attorney Brian Heberlig argued that U.S. prosecutors “began with guilt and worked backwards,” basing their claims of conspiracy on isolated incidents.
Huawei’s success, he said, is “about competition, not conspiracy. Innovation, not theft. Ordinary business dealings, not criminal conduct.”
Heberlig told reporters that the company will appeal the case.
“We believe the government’s remaining charges are equally without legal or factual merit,” Huawei said in a statement . “We will thoroughly review the relevant verdicts and take all necessary legal actions to defend our rights and interests.”
Huawei lawyer Brian Heberlig speaks to reporters outside federal court in Brooklyn, N.Y., on Nov. 24, 2026. Larry Neumeister—AP
Huawei was convicted of conspiracy to steal trade secrets from U.S. companies over two decades. Its alleged theft includes router source code from Cisco Systems, semiconductor equipment from CNEX Labs, robotic phone testing equipment from T-Mobile, antenna technology from Quintel, and networking equipment information from Fujitsu Network Communications. The jury also found Huawei and its subsidiaries guilty of violating the International Emergency Economic Powers Act and money laundering.
During the trial, which began Sept. 8, the jury watched a video that prosecutors said showed a Huawei engineer unbolting and detaching the arm of a high-speed T-Mobile testing robot and slipping it into his backpack. The engineer said he found the piece in his bag, calling the incident a “mistake,” and returned it the next day after T-Mobile reported it missing, but not before a visiting engineer from China allegedly measured and photographed the robotic arm, according to prosecutors. Huawei later fired the employee.
Prosecutors also argued that Huawei had hired a professor to gain access to a circuit board developed by CNEX.
“Huawei cultivated a culture of crime and corruption, and that crime was an important business strategy,” U.S. prosecutor Taylor Stout said in his opening statement.
Huawei’s attorneys called 15 witnesses to give evidence that the company’s success came from its own innovation. The attorneys cited the company’s 110,000-person research and development team and its over 165,000 patents. Heberlig said prosecutors had “cherry-picked” instances of employee misconduct that were not representative of Huawei’s company culture.
Prosecutors also argued that Huawei deliberately deceived global banks, including HSBC, BNP Paribas, and Standard Chartered, about its business in Iran and North Korea, which are both subject to U.S. sanctions. Huawei allegedly presented its Iran subsidiary, Skycom Tech, as an independent entity to skirt sanctions.
The jury, however, rejected the government’s assertion that Huawei had conspired in a racketeering scheme to expand its global business. If the company had been convicted of the RICO charge, it could have faced potential forfeiture of parts of its enterprise.
“It’s hard not to have profoundly mixed emotions from the verdict we just heard,” Heberlig, Huawei’s attorney, told reporters. The RICO charge, he said, “alleged that the company was corrupt from top to bottom, that it had a corporate culture and policy of cheating, stealing, and lying, and the jury found the company not guilty on that charge.”
The jury also acquitted the company of conspiring to obstruct a federal grand jury investigation.
The legal case is among the most extensive against a corporation, involving millions of documents in evidence, covering source code, financial records, and emails. Jurors spent five days, beginning Nov. 18, deliberating the case.
“Rarely has a jury had to commit so much of their personal time to a trial,” U.S. District Judge Ann Donnelly, who oversaw the case, said.
The case also took a winding path before the trial even began. It was delayed for years during the COVID-19 pandemic. In 2022, U.S. prosecutors also charged two Chinese intelligence officers with trying to bribe a U.S. government employee with $61,000 in bitcoin to steal evidence and information about the case.
The case could have ramifications on the U.S.’s relationship with China. The verdict comes days after President Donald Trump met with Chinese President Xi Jinping in Shenzhen. It also comes amid tensions over Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s affair with an alleged Chinese spy , which has renewed calls by U.S. lawmakers for tighter restrictions on A.I. chip sales to China .
Huawei, which is privately held, is one of China’s largest and most famous companies. The company reported 880.9 billion RMB ($126 billion) in revenue last year. It employs more than 200,000 employees globally and operates in more than 170 countries.
The case spawned a diplomatic crisis in 2018, when Canadian authorities detained Huawei Chief Financial Officer Meng Wanzhou, who is also the daughter of the company’s founder, at the U.S.’s request. Meng had been secretly indicted on U.S. charges of bank and wire fraud.
Meng pleaded not guilty to criminal charges and fought extradition to the U.S. while under house arrest in Vancouver for nearly three years. She entered a deferred prosecution agreement in 2021, which acknowledged that she had misled an HSBC banker about Huawei’s relationship with Skycom, after which she returned to China. A federal judge dismissed the charges against her with prejudice in December 2022. The HSBC executive Meng had met with in 2013 testified in the Brooklyn trial.
The first charges were announced as Washington and Beijing were locked in a trade war.
Since the first-term Trump Administration launched the “China Initiative” in 2018, federal prosecutors have secured convictions against a number of foreign nationals, but corporate cases have had mixed outcomes. Taiwan’s United Microelectronics pleaded guilty to stealing trade secrets in 2020, and China’s Hytera Communications pleaded guilty to conspiring to steal trade secrets in 2025. Chinese chipmaker Fujian Jinhua was acquitted in 2024. A separate federal case in Seattle against two Huawei subsidiaries has been repeatedly delayed, with a trial date set for October

articles.title_orig: U.S. chip curbs and distillation crackdown to impact Chinese AI model progress
articles.title_zh: U.S. chip curbs and distillation crackdown to impact Chinese AI model progress
articles.content_orig:
Nvidia chip sellers are seeking new buyers for the semiconductor giant's hardware, three people told CNBC, after the Trump administration tightened rules to curb Chinese companies' remote access to the most advanced artificial-intelligence systems.
Companies have put an unusually high volume of Nvidia graphics processing units, or GPUs, on the market since new measures restricting Chinese companies renting access to advanced Nvidia chips were announced on Nov. 16, the people said.
Jack Duhamel, president of AI infrastructure marketplace GPU Mart, and two people familiar with the matter told CNBC the surge in GPUs for sale was directly attributable to the new rule. Duhamel added that one company looking to sell Nvidia chips told GPU Mart the sale was related to the new rule.
The two people said it appeared chip sellers were seeking to offload them because they were originally for use in data centers in which Chinese companies would rent access. They asked not to be named because they were discussing private information.
The Department of Commerce's Bureau of Industry and Security, or BIS, announced an interim final rule as part of a clampdown on Chinese companies bypassing export controls, which effectively ban the sale of the most advanced Nvidia chips to China, by accessing them remotely in overseas data centers. The rule came into effect on Nov. 19.
Deals to find buyers for thousands of B300 GPUs, one of Nvidia's most advanced offerings, have been floated since the rule was announced, said Duhamel and one of the people.
Nvidia declined to comment. BIS did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
Nvidia has been facing increasing scrutiny from U.S. lawmakers over Chinese companies' access to its advanced chips.
The chip giant warned its customers that the proposed Remote Access Security Act — which has passed the House of Representatives but is yet to pass the Senate — would give the U.S. government broader authority to control access to cloud services, potentially exposing both parties to "legal action," sources previously told CNBC.
In July, the U.S. accused a Chinese AI lab, Moonshot AI , of accessing Nvidia chips via a facility in Thailand. CNBC reported on Nov. 5 that the company had sought access to the chips via data centers in Europe.
U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer told CNBC's "Squawk Box" on Wednesday that the new rule announced last week was intended to close "loopholes."
"For a long time, we have not allowed the sale of Blackwell chips, which are the highest AI chips or similar chips to China directly," he said.
"Some rules were issued by the Commerce Department last week to close off indirect access, either smuggling through places like Southeast Asia or remote access from data centers in third countries."
During Nvidia's third-quarter earnings call on Nov. 17, then-interim CEO Colette Kress said the company was still studying the controls, but expected performance to remain strong because demand for chips far exceeded supply.

articles.title_zh: Shein agrees to pay $100 million to settle claims of misleading customers
articles.content_orig:
Fast-fashion retailer Shein has agreed to pay $100 million to settle Federal Trade Commission allegations that it misled customers.
The FTC says the money will be used to compensate customers harmed by the company's practices.
The agency said tens of thousands of customers reported receiving their orders late, while others never received them at all. Shein allegedly failed to notify customers of shipping delays as required by law.
RELATED STORY | Fashion giant Shein facing new scrutiny from US regulators
The FTC also accused Shein of publishing positive product reviews while suppressing or deleting negative ones.
Investigators also found that some cotton Shein advertised as U.S.-grown originated in China.
Under the proposed settlement, Shein would be required to stop misrepresenting delivery times, suppressing negative reviews and making deceptive claims about its supply chain. The company would also have to provide adequate customer service.

articles.content_orig:
The Trump administration has unveiled a fresh tariff salvo on more than a dozen trading partners, with China, Vietnam, and India facing some of the steepest potential rates and mounting pressure to conclude trade deals with Washington.
The proposed tariffs, framed as curbing excess industrial capacity, start at 15% for the European Union, South Korea, Switzerland and Taiwan and rise to as much as 35% for Vietnam.
The U.S. Trade Representative's Office said it intends to cap the new duties at lower levels for countries that have completed trade deals or are still negotiating with Washington.
The overall impact on the region is likely to be limited, said Mark Williams, chief Asia economist at Capital Economics. The proposal "puts most of the targeted countries back where they were earlier in the year," he said, after the Supreme Court struck down Trump's emergency tariffs in February.
Still, the proposal could give some countries an incentive to speed up trade talks in order to lock in lower tariff rates, analysts said.
On Wednesday, U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer said that the new policy likely will not take effect for months, with a senior U.S. official saying the duties could take effect as early as January.
China faces a capped rate of 20%, on top of an existing 25% tariff imposed during President Donald Trump's first term. The rate could rise to 40% if the trade truce reached in South Korea last October is not extended beyond January, the USTR said.
Beijing has rejected Washington's claim of excess capacity while vowing to take measures necessary to protect its rights.
On Thursday, Chinese Commerce Ministry spokesperson He Yadong called on Washington to "rectify its wrongdoing and return to the right track of resolving issues through dialogue."
He was responding to Washington's plan to raise tariffs following its Section 301 investigations, while the ministry also urged the U.S. to implement $30 billion of reciprocal tariff cuts agreed by the two sides in late September.
The renewed tensions come despite several conciliatory meetings between Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping this year, as well as what Williams described as Trump's "apparent lack of concern" about allegations that Chinese technology firms have circumvented U.S. chip export controls.
The two leaders are expected to meet for a fourth time this year at the Group of 20 leaders summit in Miami in December.
"While not happy, Beijing seems prepared to live with the new rates provided that they don't exceed 20%," said Wendy Cutler, senior vice president at the Asia Society Policy Institute.
By retaining the option to raise levies if bilateral talks deteriorate, Washington is using the tariffs as leverage to "secure expected shipments of critical minerals and rare earths, and further purchases of U.S. agricultural goods," Cutler said.
Washington has warned that tariffs on Chinese goods could double to 40% if the USTR finds that Beijing is not engaging. "If the trade war did start up again, today's measures provide the U.S. with some ammunition," Williams said.
Even the sweeping actions against the other 13 trading partners appear aimed squarely at China, said Williams, who tallied that the word "China" appears 253 times in the USTR's report on Vietnam, and 315 times in the document on the European Union.
"Foremost among the 'unreasonable acts, policies, and practices' that these countries are criticised for is being slow to restrict imports and FDI from China," Williams said.
While the proposed tariffs generally lift average rates only modestly, India and Vietnam stand out because of the wider gaps between the rates they would face with and without a deal, analysts said.
India and Vietnam face proposed tariffs of 25% and 35%, respectively, but those rates could fall sharply to 17% and 20% if ongoing talks with the U.S. produce reciprocal trade agreements.
The two countries have "a strong incentive" to conclude deals with Washington to secure the lower rates, Cutler said.
Vietnam's trade ministry said Thursday that it was working with the U.S. to complete a trade deal as soon as possible, according to Reuters . India could also gain an edge over some Asian rivals through comparatively lower levies if New Delhi concludes its long-pending trade deal with Washington.
Singapore faces a similar challenge. The proposal sets a maximum potential rate of 20% on its exports, net of existing Section 301 tariffs, which could fall to 10% if it reaches an agreement on reciprocal trade with the U.S. or concludes other negotiations addressing the USTR's findings, according to Singapore's Ministry of Energy, Trade and Industry .
The ministry said it disagreed with the findings and was "very disappointed" with the proposed action, arguing that it failed to account for the structure of Singapore's economy.
Under the U.S.-Singapore Free Trade Agreement, Singapore imposes zero tariffs on U.S. goods, while the U.S. has run a trade surplus with the city-state for more than 20 years, the ministry said. That surplus grew to $33 billion in 2025 from $27 billion in 2024.
Singapore said it would submit further comments during the public consultation period and urge the USTR to reconsider.
Exemptions for semiconductors and other electronics should cushion the impact on South Korea and Taiwan, whose economies are heavily concentrated in those sectors, analysts said.
The USTR singled out South Korea for its concentration in memory-chip production and what it described as outsized government support. Yet it excluded the country's chips from the proposed excess-capacity tariffs.
Taiwan, which faces an excess-capacity tariff cap of 15%, also benefits from exemptions for other electronics, including mobile phones and networking equipment. Its effective tariff rate would rise to about 9% from 6%, Williams estimated.
— CNBC's Evelyn Cheng contributed to this report.

articles.title_orig: A Chinese consumer advocate is stranded in South Korea as a crackdown in China targets campaigners
articles.title_zh: A Chinese consumer advocate is stranded in South Korea as a crackdown in China targets campaigners
articles.content_orig:
Please refresh the page or navigate to another page on the site to be automatically logged in Please refresh your browser to be logged in
Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.
Chinese consumer rights advocate Wang Hai has spent three decades exposing counterfeit goods and seeking compensation for buyers. In recent months, he left China fearing he was a target of the authorities, but now he is stranded in South Korea with his family, facing possible deportation home.
Wang, a well-known campaigner against counterfeit goods, said China invalidated his passport and South Korean authorities rejected his asylum. The United States also revoked his tourist visa, narrowing his options for leaving South Korea and deepening his fears of being sent back to China.
Chinese authorities launched a campaign against organized crime in July, saying they would target “malicious compensation claims.” Since then, authorities have arrested at least 100 people for allegedly extorting businesses through anti-counterfeiting work or consumer compensation claims, according to official statements reviewed by The Associated Press.
Wang said the arrests made him fear he could be next, prompting him to leave a country where official Chinese media had once praised him for his role as anti-counterfeiting activist.
China’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs told The Associated Press it was not aware of Wang’s case. The Ministry of Public Security did not respond to a request for comment.
The quagmire in which Wang, 53, and his family have found themselves has drawn concerns from rights advocates over China’s efforts to target critics abroad and the narrowing options for people seeking refuge in the U.S.
“The Chinese government’s practice of transnational repression is well documented, including in South Korea,” said Yaqiu Wang, senior China researcher at Human Rights Watch, based in Washington , and “there is no doubt that the Trump administration has created a far more hostile environment for immigrants, and even visitors.”
Wang spoke to the AP from South Korea about his situation and has appealed the rejection of his asylum application in that country.
The activist fears he will end up in jail if deported to China
The activist said that he arrived in South Korea in late September with his wife, 8-year-old daughter and infant son.
Wang said he believed Chinese authorities were targeting him and that dozens of his staff members were arrested and questioned. Some remain in detention, he said. One staffer had his passport revoked while traveling from Thailand to Singapore last month, according to him.
“The very same job has suddenly morphed from being praised into something associated with organized crime — it’s absolutely surreal," said Wang.
Asked what he is afraid of if he is sent to China, Wang didn’t hesitate: “I would definitely spend the rest of my life behind bars.”
A notice reviewed by AP showed South Korean immigration authorities rejected Wang's and his family's applications for refugee status. AP also reviewed the U.S. Embassy email that revoked his visa, in which U.S. authorities told Wang that new information made him inadmissible to the U.S. or ineligible for a U.S. visa but did not provide specific details.
The U.S. State Department didn't immediately respond to the request for comment.
He was once praised as a ‘woodpecker’ rooting out fraud
Wang became a household name in China in the 1990s for exposing counterfeit goods, an increasingly widespread problem as the country’s market economy expanded rapidly and consumer protection oversight lagged.
In 1998, Wang joined a roundtable discussion with then-U.S. President Bill Clinton during his visit to Shanghai. Wang told Clinton he had been viewed as “immoral” at home, according to a White House transcript.
Chinese state media, however, largely portrayed him favorably, calling him “China’s No. 1 anti-counterfeiting activist.” Professional consumer advocates were compared to “woodpeckers,” rooting out problems in the marketplace.
Wang ran a rights-protection company in Beijing for about 30 years and a testing laboratory supporting anti-counterfeiting work for five years. He said both were forced to close after many of his staff, including three lawyers, were arrested in September.
The closure of his offices came after China launched its campaign against organized crime. Authorities said some people were using consumer complaints, lawsuits or threats of exposure to extort money from businesses through what officials called “malicious compensation claims.”
Some lawyers say consumer rights advocates play a positive role by exposing illegal practices, pressing businesses to address problems and helping authorities enforce regulations.
“The fact that some individuals engage in these activities as a profession or as a source of income does not invalidate the legitimacy of such social oversight itself,” said Zhang Yansheng, a Beijing-based lawyer.
After fleeing China, Wang seeks a new home with freedom
Wang’s consumer advocacy began more than three decades ago, when he suspected two pairs of Sony headphones he bought at a Beijing department store were counterfeit. He bought the remaining 10 pairs and secured compensation of twice the purchase price. It was widely celebrated on Chinese state media as a pioneering case of consumer activism.
He went on to run his own company and testing lab, helping consumers seek compensation and pushing for stronger consumer protections.
Wang and other advocates also pushed for a minimum compensation payment of 500 yuan ($75) for consumers, a proposal later incorporated into a revised consumer protection law in 2013.
His most recent case involved helping cherry farmers in the northeastern city of Dalian get compensation after they bought fake pesticide. He said Dalian police later arrested and detained around four dozens of people including the cherry farmers, two lawyers who represented the farmers, and Wang's staff.
Wang said he has since focused on researching asylum options and hopes to settle in the U.S., Canada, Britain, Australia or New Zealand, seeking what he called “real law enforcement and freedom” to “get away from China's transnational repression.”
After his U.S. visa was revoked, Wang is seeking resettlement in Canada with the help of a human rights organization.
Fearing arrest by Chinese authorities even outside China, he said he and his family mostly stay indoors in South Korea. He said his bank accounts in China have been frozen, leaving the family in financial difficulty, and his 8-year-old daughter is struggling with her mental health because she cannot attend school.

articles.title_orig: At least 31 killed in Egypt vehicle fire, Health Ministry says
articles.title_zh: At least 31 killed in Egypt vehicle fire, Health Ministry says
articles.content_orig:
At least 31 people were ⁠⁠killed, and ⁠⁠another 21 were injured when a vehicle carrying ‌‌petroleum products overturned and caught fire on a major ring ⁠⁠⁠⁠road in the Egyptian capital, Cairo, the ⁠Ministry of Health said on Wednesday.
The fire broke out above a tunnel in the al-Warak neighbourhood of Giza’s Imbabah district. The ring road connects key highways across Greater Cairo, linking the governorates of Cairo, ‌‌Giza and Qalyubia.
Local media reported that a truck swerved and hit the central reservation as it overturned, triggering an explosion. The fire has since been extinguished, according to local media.
Egypt’s public prosecutor announced an investigation into the crash and ordered the collection of DNA samples from the victims’ bodies. The judicial office also said 27 vehicles were burned.
The Health Ministry said 39 ambulances were sent to the site of the incident and that the injured were transferred to nearby hospitals.
Health Minister Khaled Abdel Ghaffar said he would head to the crash scene himself.
The official spokesman for the Egyptian presidency said President Abdel Fattah el-Sisi “expresses his sincere condolences and sincere sympathy to the families of the victims” and wished them a speedy recovery.
According to an Egyptian Cabinet statement, Prime Minister Mostafa Madbouly offered his condolences to the victims’ families and ordered that their medical expenses be covered by the state.
“The Ministry of Health and Population continues to closely monitor the situation and coordinate with the relevant authorities to ensure that the necessary medical care is provided to the injured,” a ministry statement read.

articles.title_orig: Elon Musk, SpaceX pledge major stock donations to active Trump Accounts
articles.title_zh: Elon Musk, SpaceX pledge major stock donations to active Trump Accounts
articles.content_orig:
Former Deputy Treasury Secretary Michael Faulkender analyzes the potential expansion of Trump accounts for adults. He also weighs in on the challenges China's domestic economy is facing.
SpaceX announced Wednesday that it will contribute one share of its stock to every currently active Trump Account, with CEO Elon Musk pledging to personally match the company's donation.
The aerospace company's commitment follows Musk's pledge earlier this year to give every child in America a share of the company.
Musk later elaborated on the planned stock giveaway in a post on X Wednesday evening, saying every child in America would receive an additional share from him personally.
"Every child in America will receive two SpaceX shares, one from the company and one from me personally," Musk wrote.
TRUMP ACCOUNTS HIT MAJOR MILESTONE AS FAMILY CONTRIBUTIONS SURPASS $1 BILLION
SpaceX CEO Elon Musk pledged to personally match the company's planned donation of one share of stock to every currently active Trump Account. (Getty Images / Getty Images)
SpaceX said the planned contribution, which could be worth billions of dollars, would give the next generation of Americans a stake in the company's future.
"SpaceX is building the infrastructure of the future and working to make life multiplanetary," the company said in a statement. "We believe ownership of the company creating these systems should extend to the next generation of Americans for their long-term benefit."
SpaceX, whose shares were trading just above $127 Wednesday, said it would contribute one newly issued share of its Class A common stock to every currently active Trump Account.
SpaceX President and Chief Operating Officer Gwynne Shotwell also announced a separate personal donation of more than 2 million shares of the company's stock.
Musk pledged last month to give every child in America a share of SpaceX in 2027, although he did not provide details at the time about how the proposed giveaway would work.
"Next year, I will give one of my SpaceX shares to every kid in America. This will be the first of many," Musk wrote on X in October.
SpaceX confirmed Wednesday that his latest commitment is part of that pledge.
‘DATA CENTERS IN SPACE’: FCC CLEARS SPACEX FOR 1M SATELLITES TO ‘EXTEND AMERICA’S LEAD IN SUPERINTELLIGENCE’
SpaceX announced Wednesday that it would contribute one newly issued share of its Class A common stock to every currently active Trump Account. (Alisha Jucevic/Bloomberg via Getty Images / Getty Images)
The announcement comes just one day after the Treasury Department revealed that contributions from friends and family members to Trump Accounts had surpassed $1 billion.
With the holiday season approaching, the pledged contributions represent another boost for the program, which provides tax-advantaged investment accounts for American children under 18 with valid Social Security numbers.
More than 3 million friends and family members have contributed to individual accounts, with total deposits exceeding $9 billion when philanthropic gifts and federal seed contributions are included, according to a Treasury Department statement provided to FOX Business.
Children born between Jan. 1, 2025, and Dec. 31, 2028, are eligible for a one-time $1,000 seed contribution from the federal government.
While Trump Accounts have been created for eligible children under 18, parents and guardians must claim the accounts before they can manage them or enable contributions.
GET FOX BUSINESS ON THE GO BY CLICKING HERE
Trump Accounts are set to receive additional contributions from SpaceX and Elon Musk after total deposits in the children's investment program surpassed $9 billion. (Mandel NGAN / AFP / Getty Images)
The Treasury Department announced last month that approximately 70 million Trump Accounts had been established for eligible children, although it was not immediately clear how many had been activated.
Fox Business reached out to SpaceX for comment.

articles.title_orig: Who pays the new EU taxes? A breakdown of who will foot the bill
articles.title_zh: Who pays the new EU taxes? A breakdown of who will foot the bill
articles.content_orig:
EU leaders are engaged in intense discussion over the bloc's new seven-year budget before the end of the year, with member states butting heads over the overall size, spending priorities and how to finance it.
In terms of new resources Brussels intends to tap into, European Council President Antonio Costa proposed an ambitious mix of EU-wide taxes meant to generate about €60bn in revenue each year.
But who pays the bill? With Costa's compromise, the European Commission circulated an updated estimate of how much each Europe-wide tax is meant to generate, and which countries will bear most of the costs.
Between 2028 and 2034, Germany would be by far the country paying the highest share of EU taxes, with over €13bn in current prices, followed by Italy with €8bn. Despite being the bloc's second-largest economy, France merely ranks third, which explains Paris' strong support for new own resources.
However, the asymmetrical contribution to own resources is best understood in terms of what they would otherwise pay in national contributions based on their Gross National Income (GNI).
Costa's proposal made several adjustments to the EU taxes, mostly to accommodate objections from member states from central and eastern Europe, leaving southern European countries to pay the highest share.
On average, the tax of €2.25 per kilogram of uncollected electronic waste is by far the one expected to yield more revenues, with over €20bn expected per year, despite it being relatively less controversial than the Emissions Trading System (ETS), the Tobacco Tax or the digital levy.
While the e-waste contribution is the largest for most member states, how much each own resource will weigh on the national governments varies considerably, shaping the positioning of the member states.
The revenues expected from each tax are not fixed due to a number of reasons, including the fact that several of them will be adjusted for inflation.
The Commission projects the yields might significantly increase over time, with the Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism (CBAM), a tax on imports of carbon-intensive products, expected to more than double its revenues by 2034.
For the tax of €1.25 per kilogram of non-recycled plastic packaging waste, over half of the revenues are expected to come from the EU's four largest member states, France, Germany, Italy and Spain.
Similarly, the four EU countries would also account for over 60% of the revenues coming from an EU-wide digital services tax. France, Italy and Spain already have a digital levy at the national level, meaning they would lose these revenues in favour of Brussels.
The yields of the tobacco excise duty are also highly geographically concentrated, but in this case there is a less linear relation with the member states' population and reflects more national consumption habits and national excise duty levels.
Luxembourg, for instance, would make a significant contribution despite its relatively tiny size, as it sells large volumes of cigarettes and related products to consumers from neighbouring countries thanks to its lower prices.
For the tax on e-waste, which envisages a contribution from member states based on the share of electronic devices produced on their territory that are recycled, over 60% of the revenues would come from Germany, Italy and France, the EU's manufacturing powerhouses. By contrast, the Commission estimates Bulgaria would have to pay zero.
Giving 30% of the revenues generated from the Emissions Trading System (ETS), a carbon market for CO2-intensive industries, would be particularly advantageous for France, which would be in fourth position in terms of contribution, whilst it would penalise countries like Poland and Bulgaria compared to their economic size.
Italy would be the first payer for the Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism (CBAM), with Belgium and Poland also punching above their weight in terms of contributions.
